extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, and appellate practitioners (people analyzing patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for determining whether claimed subject matter falls within the statutory categories of patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter), with particular application to claims to transitory signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories requirement (§ 101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter ... may obtain a patent therefor (35 U.S.C. § 101). The claimed subject matter must fall into at least one of these four categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The four-category language is the explicit scope of patentable subject matter; if a claim covers material not found in any of the four categories it falls outside § 101 even if new and useful. Historical context and precedent inform the meaning of each category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process (statutory) requires acts or steps
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'process' is a mode of treatment of certain materials to produce a given result; it is an act, or a series of acts, performed upon the subject-matter to be transformed and reduced to a different state or thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities (Cochrane v. Deener, Gottschalk v. Benson, In re Kollar, NTP v. RIM) hold that a process must be carried out (i.e., recite acts/steps). Merely describing a product by reference to the process that made it (product-by-process) does not make the claim a 'process' for § 101 purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims remain product claims (do not convert to process)
rubrics_metrics.description: A product-by-process claim defines a product at least in part by the method or process by which it is made; such claims are still directed to the ultimate product, not the underlying process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a claim recites an encoding process, that recitation does not transform a claim to the resulting signal into a process claim; the claim must be considered as to the product it covers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine must be a concrete thing with parts/devices
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'machine' is a concrete thing, consisting of parts, or of certain devices and combination of devices; includes mechanical devices or combinations of powers and devices to perform some function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitory electromagnetic or electrical signals, though physical, lack 'parts' or 'devices' in the mechanical sense and therefore are not 'machines' under § 101. Apparatus that generates or processes signals, however, may be machines and are separately claimable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture defined as production of articles for use by giving new form/qualities/properties
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'manufacture' involves the production of articles for use from raw or prepared materials by giving to these materials new forms, qualities, properties, or combinations (American Fruit Growers / Chakrabarty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This term is typically applied to tangible articles or commodities. A transitory signal lacking permanence or tangible commodity-like form is unlikely to qualify as a 'manufacture.' The court relies on the Supreme Court's Fruit Growers/Chakrabarty definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of matter requires compositions/mixtures of substances
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Composition of matter' means compositions of two or more substances and composite articles, whether the result of chemical union or mechanical mixture — e.g., gases, fluids, powders, solids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transient electrical or electromagnetic fluctuations are not chemical unions or typical forms of 'composition of matter' and thus do not meet this category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction is a threshold legal question
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is a question of law reviewed de novo and must be resolved before or as part of the § 101 analysis; understanding claim scope can determine whether the claim fits a statutory category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret whether claim terms (e.g., 'signal') require a physical carrier and whether dependent claims add physical limitations. Courts construe claims to determine if some physical carrier is required or if the claim could cover abstract data.

rubrics_metrics.name: A 'signal' claim requires some physical carrier to convey information
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'signal' implies signaling—the conveyance of information—and to convey information to a recipient a physical carrier (e.g., electromagnetic wave, electrical signal, pulses in fiber) is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a physical carrier is required, the claims need not specify what carrier; any tangible means of information carriage will suffice so long as a recipient can understand the message. This limits claims to physical instances but not to particular media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitory, propagating signals (ephemeral transmissions) are not patentable subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitory electrical and electromagnetic signals propagating through a medium are not encompassed by any of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) and thus are not patentable under § 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court emphasizes the fleeting, non-permanent character of such signals, and their lack of tangible article-like characteristics; storage of the signal on a medium is a different category (e.g., storage medium claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangibility/permanence requirement for 'manufacture' (practical consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a 'manufacture' under the Fruit Growers/Chakrabarty definition, the claimed subject should result in an 'article' or commodity with some degree of permanence/physical form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the signal may be man-made and physical in a sense, the absence of permanence during transmission and lack of commodity-like status weigh against finding 'manufacture.' A stored signal on a medium (e.g., Claim 15 storage medium) may qualify differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: State Street guidance — focus on essential characteristics and utility but still must fit a statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should look to the essential characteristics and practical utility of the subject matter rather than be preoccupied with pigeonholing among the four categories; nonetheless the subject matter must fall into at least one statutory category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it is clear a claim satisfies a statutory category, courts need not decide which one; however, where a claim may fall into none, the court must analyze each statutory category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed matter doctrine / information-on-medium requires functional relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: When the only difference between prior art and a claimed storage medium is the information stored thereon (printed matter), the stored information lacks patentable weight unless there is a new functional relationship between the printed matter and the substrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to information encoded on a tangible medium may be patentable if the information imposes a physical organization or functional improvement (Lowry). Otherwise, the doctrine often operates under § 103 to reject such claims as obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea exclusion (algorithmic/mathematical principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract mathematical algorithms or principles (e.g., conversion algorithms) that are so general as to cover known and unknown uses are not patentable subject matter (Gottschalk v. Benson; Parker v. Flook).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even useful algorithms may be unpatentable if the claim effectively covers an abstract idea without being tied to a statutory category or a specific physical application; presence of a physical manifestation may affect analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for § 101 and claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a claim is valid under § 101 is a question of law reviewed de novo; claim construction is likewise a question of law reviewed de novo on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate review treats these legal determinations without deference, so precise articulation and analysis of claim terms and statutory meaning is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus claims vs. signal claims: apparatus that generates signals may be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: While transitory signals themselves may be unpatentable, apparatus (machines) that generate, receive, process, or store signals can be patentable as machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim drafting that recites physical structure (devices, encoders, storage media) rather than just the transient signal can place the subject matter within a statutory category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad claim scope when claims specify only informational content
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that limit only the informational content (e.g., 'a signal encoded in accordance with a given encoding process') without tying the claim to a particular physical medium or structural features may be read to cover intangible strings of data or many forms of carriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such breadth can create § 101 vulnerability; claim drafters should consider adding physical or structural limitations to avoid claims that purport to cover abstract or purely informational entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility (new and useful) remains a separate limitation relevant to § 101 analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory requirement that an invention be 'new and useful' informs whether claimed subject matter is sufficiently concrete and direct in its benefit to qualify as patent-eligible (Brenner v. Manson; In re Fisher).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims whose only contribution is information content without a functional technological effect may fail utility or be treated via printed matter/obviousness doctrines; court distinguishes between useful technological applications and mere abstract information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and precedent-based interpretive constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation of § 101 categories draws on historical statutory language and Supreme Court precedent (e.g., Patent Acts of 1790/1793/1836, legislative history of 1952 Act, Burr, Cochrane, Chakrabarty, Morse, Benson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts apply these interpretive anchors (definitions and past holdings) when deciding whether novel technologies fall within statutory categories; differing views (concurring/dissenting opinions) highlight unresolved doctrinal boundaries.
